Meerut to Get ₹200-Crore Critical Minerals and Rare Earth Refinery, 1,300 Jobs Expected
The proposed facility will recover critical minerals such as lithium, cobalt and nickel from used lithium-ion batteries
Uttar Pradesh is set to strengthen its position in advanced materials recycling with a proposed ₹200-crore critical minerals and rare earth refinery in Meerut. Deep-tech startup Circulogy Cleantech Private Limited has signed a memorandum of understanding (MoU) with Invest UP for the proposed project.
The facility is expected to generate approximately 300 direct and 1,000 indirect employment opportunities, taking the anticipated employment impact to around 1,300 jobs. The project is planned to be developed in phases, with a targeted annual processing capacity of 10,000 tonnes at full scale.
The refinery will focus on recovering valuable materials from end-of-life lithium-ion batteries, electronic waste and used permanent magnets, helping convert discarded products into resources for industrial use.
Lithium, Cobalt and Nickel Recovery in Focus
The proposed facility will recover critical minerals such as lithium, cobalt and nickel from used lithium-ion batteries. These materials are essential for battery manufacturing, electric vehicles, energy storage systems and several electronics applications.
The project also envisages recovering rare earth elements, including neodymium, dysprosium and terbium, from discarded permanent magnets used in electronic equipment, hard drives and electric vehicle motors.
Rare earth elements are important for high-performance motors, renewable energy technologies, electronics and several strategic applications. Developing domestic recovery capabilities could help India diversify its sources of these materials and strengthen its recycling ecosystem.
Boost to India’s Critical Minerals Strategy
India’s growing electric vehicle, renewable energy and electronics industries are increasing the importance of securing reliable supplies of critical minerals. Dependence on imported materials remains a strategic concern for manufacturers and policymakers.
The proposed Meerut refinery could contribute to domestic mineral recovery by extracting valuable materials from products that would otherwise enter waste streams. Such facilities can complement conventional mining by recovering resources already present in batteries, electronic equipment and industrial components.
The project also aligns with the broader policy push to strengthen India’s critical minerals value chain, including exploration, processing, recycling and the recovery of materials from end-of-life products.
However, the project’s eventual contribution to reducing import dependence will depend on its commissioning, actual recovery rates, feedstock availability and the commercial scale of operations.
Invest UP to Facilitate Project Development
The MoU with Invest UP is intended to facilitate the proposed investment and support the company in navigating applicable approvals and clearances. Assistance in accessing relevant central and state government incentives may also be available, subject to eligibility and prevailing rules.
The project represents an opportunity to expand technology-led industrial activity in western Uttar Pradesh. Critical mineral recycling combines waste management with resource recovery, creating potential opportunities for specialised processing, logistics and associated industrial services.
1,300 Employment Opportunities Expected
The proposed investment is expected to create around 300 direct jobs and 1,000 indirect jobs. The indirect employment impact could extend to supply chains, collection and transportation of used batteries and electronic waste, and supporting industrial services.
The targeted capacity of 10,000 tonnes per year would position the proposed facility as a significant recycling project, provided it achieves its planned scale of operations.
The next milestones will be the development of the facility, completion of necessary approvals, commissioning and the commencement of commercial operations. These stages will determine when the anticipated employment and industrial benefits begin to materialise.
For Uttar Pradesh, the project signals an opportunity to participate in the emerging market for critical mineral recovery and advanced materials recycling, an area of growing importance to India’s manufacturing and clean-energy ambitions.

articles.title: Rainbow Rare Earths highlights fundamental shift in attitudes toward critical minerals - Proactive financial news
articles.summary: Rainbow Rare Earths highlights fundamental shift in attitudes toward critical minerals  Proactive financial news
articles.full_text:
Rainbow Rare Earths Ltd (LSE:RBW, OTC:RBWRF, FRA:RR1) describes 2026 as a 'defining period' which has seen a fundamental shift in Western attitudes towards critical minerals.
Chairman Adonis Pouroulis argues that securing rare earth supplies outside China has become a permanent priority for governments and industry.
In the company's annual results statement, chairman Adonis Pouroulis said China's tightening export controls had exposed the vulnerability of global supply chains, prompting Western governments to introduce price support mechanisms, strategic stockpiles and direct investment in alternative sources.
He pointed to a widening price divide between heavy rare earths sold inside China and material available to Western buyers as evidence of the changing market.
"Against this backdrop, the case for new, diversified, responsibly produced sources of REE outside China has never been stronger," Pouroulis said.
Rainbow believes its strategy of recovering rare earth elements from phosphogypsum, a waste product of fertiliser production, positions it to benefit from this shift without the costs associated with conventional hard-rock mining.
Reviewing progress during the financial year ended 30 June 2026, the company highlighted advances at its flagship Phalaborwa project in South Africa, where 75% of the processing flowsheet had reached a stage suitable for detailed engineering.
It also pointed to its selection of Neo Performance Materials as a technical and prospective offtake partner, subject to binding agreements, and progress at the Uberaba project in Brazil, where an economic assessment indicated a US$916 million post-tax net present value.
Rainbow finished the financial year with US$12.9 million in cash, compared with US$3.9 million a year earlier, following an £11.1 million equity placing in April. Its annual loss widened to US$7.5 million from US$3.2 million, largely reflecting a non-cash revaluation of its Ecora royalty liability.
The company currently targets publication of a Phalaborwa pre-feasibility study in the fourth quarter of 2026, followed by a definitive feasibility study in the first half of 2027.
It is expected to require additional funding in the third quarter of 2027, with the unsecured financing requirement identified as a material going-concern uncertainty.

New Delhi: Meerut-based deep tech startup Circulology Cleantech Private Limited has planned to invest around Rs 200 crore in the state. The company has signed an MoU with Invest UP to set up a lithium-ion battery and rare earth refinery in Meerut. The project will provide direct employment to about 300 people and indirect employment to 1,000 people.
Sumit Mahajan, CEO of UP Startup Mission, said that the Yogi government is emphasizing on encouraging local entrepreneurs, startups and tech-based industries. In this direction, efforts are being made to convert new ideas into business projects in the state through the UP Startup Mission and provide opportunities to the startups to move forward. The proposed project in Meerut is also an important step towards connecting the local startups of the state with large industrial investment. This is expected to boost the development of industries based on new technology in Western Uttar Pradesh.
He said that the refinery of Circularity will be developed in a phased manner. It plans to process 10,000 tons of material every year after reaching full capacity. Critical minerals such as lithium, cobalt and nickel will be recovered from the lithium-ion batteries used in the refinery. In addition, rare earth elements such as neodymium, dysprosium and terbium will also be extracted from old permanent magnets used in electronic devices, hard drives and motors of electric vehicles. These minerals are used in electric vehicles, renewable energy, electronics and defence. From batteries for electric vehicles to modern technological equipment and plants for power generation, they play an important role. Reclaiming these minerals from old batteries and equipment can help in better utilization of resources as well as strengthen the domestic supply system.
The CEO pointed out that imports account for almost the entire domestic requirement of lithium, cobalt and nickel. Similarly, dependence on imports is also a major challenge in the supply of rare earth magnets. In such a situation, it has become necessary to develop recycling and refining capacity within the country. The Government of India has also taken several steps to promote self-reliance in the field of critical minerals. Under the National Critical Minerals Mission, emphasis is being laid on strengthening the entire supply chain of critical minerals. It also includes an incentive scheme of Rs 1,500 crore to incentivize recycling of critical minerals from e-waste and used batteries.
Further, in November 2025, the Union Cabinet had approved a Rs 7,280 crore scheme to promote the manufacturing of rare earth permanent magnets in India. The scheme aims to develop a production capacity of 6,000 tonnes annually. Recycled minerals and rare earth oxides from Circulogy’s proposed refinery can prove useful for such domestic industrial supply chains. Meerut-based Circularology is a DPIIT-accredited deep tech startup that works on circular economy.
The company has received support from the UP Startup Mission under the startup ecosystem of Uttar Pradesh. Under the MoU, the Yogi government will facilitate in obtaining necessary approvals and clearances. Also, the project will also be supported in getting the benefits of the incentive schemes of the Central and State Government as per the applicable rules. The proposed project, worth about Rs 200 crore, has the potential to create new employment opportunities along with the expansion of emerging tech industries in the state. With this, Meerut’s identity can develop into new areas like Critical Mineral Recycling and Refining along with traditional industrial activities.

MP Materials is a top domestic supplier of vital rare-earth and permanent magnets
Rare-earth elements include neodymium-praseodymium (NdPr), dysprosium (Dy), terbium (Tb), gadolinium, and samarium, which are crucial inputs for high-performance permanent magnets (NdFeB magnets). These magnets are unique because they offer high torque-to-weight and power density and are used in electric-vehicle drive motors, humanoid robots, industrial automation, defense guidance systems, and drones.
According to research from The Motley Fool, China controls most rare-earth mining and processing, giving it significant leverage in trade negotiations. MP owns and operates the Mountain Pass Mine in California. This is the only scaled rare-earth mining and processing site in the U.S., which gives MP a first-mover advantage over others looking to build their own mine-to-magnet businesses.
In support of this, the Department of Defense (DoD) awarded MP Materials a price protection agreement that guarantees a $110/kilogram price floor for NdPr produced at Mountain Pass. The move helps shield MP Materials from China's predatory pricing, which has historically used state subsidies to drive down rare-earth prices and push Western producers into bankruptcy. This practice caused Mountain Pass's previous owners to go bankrupt in 2015.
MP Materials' offtake agreement with the DoD also includes a 10-year agreement that guarantees at least $140 million of annual EBITDA for MP's second magnet campus. MP also has long-term supply agreements with Apple and General Motors, and has also signed a multi-year contract with an unnamed major U.S. aerospace manufacturer for separated gadolinium oxide.
Freeport-McMoRan benefits from the power grid build-out
While rare-earth elements are vital for permanent magnets, copper is known as the "metal of electrification" for its electrical and thermal conductivity and its role in the power grid. Roughly 65% of copper is consumed in applications that deliver or use electricity. Copper is a key component in data centers, power-grid modernization, and related infrastructure. According to S&P Global, global copper demand could grow by 50% by 2040.
Freeport-McMoRan is one of the world's largest publicly traded copper producers, owning and operating tier-1 assets in North America, South America, and Indonesia. The company dominates the U.S. market, accounting for about 70% of the country's refined copper production, with operations in Arizona, Texas, and New Mexico.

Additionally, the U.S. Secretary of Commerce is considering requirements that 25% of copper cathode and concentrate products produced in the U.S. be sold domestically by 2027.

articles.title: Chile’s rare earth ambitions hit refining bottleneck - Mining.com
articles.summary: Chile’s rare earth ambitions hit refining bottleneck  Mining.com
articles.full_text:
Chile’s push to become a major rare earth supplier faces a costly industrial gap as the country advances mining and metal production projects without the separation capacity needed to build an integrated supply chain, according to a new study by GEM Mining Consulting.
The challenge came into focus with the Oct. 7 inauguration of a demonstration plant at Huachipato in Talcahuano, where Aclara Metals, a 50-50 joint venture between Aclara Resources (TSX: ARA) and Chilean industrial group CAP, is testing technology to convert rare earth oxides into metals and alloys. The facility can produce up to 175 kg of metal daily through molten salt electrolysis, targeting purity of at least 99.5%.
The plant will initially process neodymium and praseodymium (NdPr), with dysprosium potentially added later. GEM’s study, Rare Earths in Chile: What if the Biggest Opportunity Comes After the Mine?, warns that developing metallurgical expertise without domestic separation facilities could leave Chile dependent on overseas processors.
The findings underscore a broader challenge for countries seeking alternatives to China, which controls approximately 65% of global magnetic rare earth mining, 91% of separation and refining, and 94% of permanent magnet manufacturing, according to International Energy Agency data cited by GEM. The greatest opportunity may therefore lie in processing minerals rather than simply extracting more of them.
Missing link
GEM estimates that committed global mining supply could reach 107% of projected magnetic rare earth requirements by 2035. Yet existing and announced projects outside China could satisfy only 25% of non-Chinese separation requirements and less than 20% of magnet demand, even as mining capacity expands.
The supply chain begins with concentrates or carbonates, which undergo chemical separation to produce individual rare earth oxides or combinations such as NdPr oxide. Metallization converts those products into metals for alloys and permanent magnets used in electric vehicles, wind turbines and industrial equipment.
Chile has projects at both ends of that process, but GEM identified no industrial-scale domestic separation operation or permanent magnet manufacturing facility.
Aclara’s Penco Module in the Biobío region received environmental approval in June. An updated preliminary economic assessment released this week values the project at $243 million (C$344 million). The company plans to recover rare earths from ionic clay deposits but still requires additional permits and faces community opposition.
In a February 2022 citizen-organized consultation involving more than 7,400 participants, 99% voted against the proposed development, according to Diario Concepción.
Chilean Cobalt Corp. is also advancing its NeoRe project, having completed a second development phase in September that included a preliminary resource estimate and conceptual economic assessment. Heavy rare earths represent approximately 30% of its estimated resource basket, while initial carbonate production of about 50 tonnes annually is targeted from early 2027, subject to technical validation, permitting and financing.
Neither development currently establishes a complete domestic supply chain. Aclara intends to separate carbonates from its Chilean and Brazilian operations at a proposed facility in Louisiana, US, where it is also considering commercial-scale metals and alloys production informed by the Huachipato trials.
Processing economics
Building competitive refining capacity remains difficult. GEM estimates that rare earth processing plants outside China can face capital costs 20% to more than 150% higher than Chinese competitors, alongside operating expenses approximately 50% greater.
NdPr oxide traded at about $95 per kg in Europe and North America in August 2026 on a cost, insurance and freight basis, according to Benchmark Mineral Intelligence data cited by GEM.
That compares with a $110-per-kg price floor under a 2025 agreement between MP Materials and the US Department of Defense. Australian producer Lynas also secured a proposed $110-per-kg minimum price under a March 2026 supply arrangement with the US government. Although these arrangements differ from spot market pricing, they illustrate the government support needed to encourage alternative processing capacity.
Chile is seeking to capitalize on that strategic shift. Rare earths are included in its national critical minerals strategy, which aims to diversify the country’s mineral industry beyond copper and lithium. In March, Chile also signed a bilateral agreement with the US to strengthen cooperation on rare earth exploitation and commercialization, supporting efforts to develop supply chains outside China.
The country’s vast copper mining industry offers another potential source of feedstock. Hundreds of historical tailings deposits contain material that could yield critical minerals, including rare earth elements, through new recovery technologies.
Chile’s economic development agency Corfo has supported initiatives offering approximately $3 million to $4 million in project funding to investigate extracting cobalt and rare earths from mining waste, potentially turning legacy environmental liabilities into valuable resources.
GEM’s study warns that tailings recovery must still demonstrate viable extraction economics and produce material suitable for downstream separation. Additional feedstock alone would not eliminate the industry’s processing constraints.
The Huachipato facility, located at a steelmaking complex that ceased operations in September 2024, provides an industrial setting for testing advanced metallurgy. Its demonstration-scale output, however, does not establish the commercial viability of a larger operation.
GEM identifies adequate feedstock, proven technology, competitive plant capacity, customer qualification and long-term supply and offtake agreements as essential conditions for investment.
Chile’s next challenge is to determine whether it can establish commercially sustainable separation and manufacturing operations at home, capturing more value from its mineral resources rather than transferring dependence from Chinese processors to facilities elsewhere.

articles.title: South Asia's Critical Minerals Moment: India, Pakistan, and U.S. Diversification Efforts - Asia Society
articles.summary: South Asia's Critical Minerals Moment: India, Pakistan, and U.S. Diversification Efforts  Asia Society
articles.full_text:
As the United States prioritizes diversification of critical minerals supply chains, South Asia warrants attention as regional players and partners like India and Pakistan offer demand, scale, and resources that could help advance U.S. ongoing efforts.
Critical minerals today sit at the foundation of advanced manufacturing, clean energy, artificial intelligence (AI), and defense technologies. For the Trump administration, reducing strategic dependence on China for these key commodities has become an increasingly important policy priority of its economic security, reflected in recent bilateral trade deals as well as in plurilateral initiatives launched over the past year, including Pax Silica, the Quad Critical Minerals Initiative, and the Forum on Resource Geostrategic Engagement (FORGE). Through these efforts, the United States aims to bring trusted partners and resource-rich countries into more resilient supply chains so that no single country maintains the ability to exercise disproportionate advantage over the others.
This is where South Asia warrants focus, especially India and Pakistan. The two countries hold mineral resources, industrial capability, large workforce, market scale, or some combination of these, making them viable partners. Yet neither country has fully realized these advantages into globally competitive value chains. The two countries also offer different strengths and are at different stages of their critical minerals sector development. India is a midstream and demand bet: its value depends on whether a sizable resource base and a large industrial market can be turned into processing and manufacturing capacity. Pakistan, on the other hand, represents an upstream investment opportunity, with significant untapped mining potential and an active push to attract U.S. investment, albeit at a heavy security premium.
The Chokepoint and South Asia's Paradox
A country may be geologically endowed but remain deeply vulnerable if it lacks the capability to process, refine, and convert these resources into commercially usable materials. That is where China's position is hardest to dislodge. China's April 2025 export controls on heavy rare earths and magnets, imposed in response to U.S. tariffs, showed how quickly that concentration can be turned into strategic leverage. The lesson for policymakers is that minerals physically available across the globe can still be hostage to whoever controls the processing and refining chokepoints.
The International Energy Agency (IEA) estimates that China's share of rare earth refining fell from above 90% in 2023 to 85% in 2025, largely owing to projects advancing in the United States and Malaysia, and could reach 70% by 2035 if all planned projects proceed. The movement toward diversification is happening, although gradually given the nature of the industry, and it also depends on sustained financial investment.
South Asia is no alternative to China’s strong hold. The regional countries will not change China's share of refining, at least not in the near term. Nevertheless, countries like India and Pakistan bring in value through optionality for the United States, offering a large market that can make diversified processing financeable, and helping set the standards for what counts as trusted supply.
The region also presents a paradox. Economies, like India, with ambitions to become major manufacturing and technology powers remain heavily dependent on imported minerals and intermediate products. Demand has outpaced domestic capability, and for years, importing was a cheaper option, given how capital-intensive and politically complex mines and refineries are. Each country has also faced its own limits, from security conditions and constraints on private participation to environmental concerns and thin geological exploration. Governments are now recognizing the economic cost of that gap between potential and production and are consequently looking to change that.
India, for example, is working to build a more integrated critical minerals ecosystem: expanding domestic exploration, developing processing and refining capacity, strengthening recycling and recovery, acquiring overseas mineral assets, and ultimately linking mineral security and development to its ambitions in manufacturing, clean energy, defense, and advanced technology.
Pakistan, by contrast, is approaching its mineral potential much more from the perspective of resource and economic development and attracting foreign investment. Its challenge, and opportunity, is to convert an underdeveloped and underleveraged mineral base into a credible platform for exploration, mining, processing, and eventually an export powerhouse. This will require significant investment coupled with investor confidence.
Both, therefore, have the potential to become relevant to increasingly diversified global supply chains and valuable partners for Washington. India remains a key strategic partner of the United States, both bilaterally and within the Indo-Pacific, despite the current strain in ties; and the reset in U.S.-Pakistan ties over the past year has enabled grounds for developing broad-based cooperation, including on critical minerals.
India
India’s critical minerals sector development is tied to its wider ambitions: to become a developed economy by 2047, expand domestic defense production, accelerate the clean energy transition, and establish itself as a major manufacturing hub. It has identified 30 minerals as critical, and those ambitions and underlying demands are advancing faster than the country’s domestic capabilities. India remains 100% import-reliant for lithium, cobalt, and nickel; and China supplied roughly 60% to 80%, by value, of its permanent magnet imports between 2022 and 2025. Domestic magnet production also remains at a preliminary stage.
India has moved from recognizing this vulnerability to building an institutional response. Legal reform, block auctions, and a magnet manufacturing push were followed by the National Critical Mineral Mission (NCMM) in January 2025, a seven-year effort covering the value chain from exploration through processing and recycling. Abroad, Khanij Bidesh India Limited (KABIL) leads the acquisition of overseas assets. New Delhi, over recent years, has also built a wide network of critical minerals partnerships with like-minded countries. This includes a critical minerals investment partnership with Australia, an agreement on lithium exploration projects in Argentina, and a comprehensive economic partnership under negotiation with Chile. India and Japan also reached a memorandum of cooperation during Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi's July 2026 visit covering joint investment in exploration and processing.
However, a growing list of agreements will not right away lead to a supply chain advantage. India recognizes that the gap is in processing and refining, and closing it requires more than acquisition, demand, and capital. It requires access to separation and refining technology as well as the skills to run it, which remain concentrated in China, and are areas where India could work with like-minded countries including Indo-Pacific partners.
This is also precisely where Washington's interests and India's converge. Electric vehicles, renewable energy, and defense production give India a domestic market large enough to underwrite midstream plants. India's participation in Pax Silica and the Quad Critical Minerals Initiative, along with the U.S.-India Critical Minerals Framework and the U.S.-India AI Opportunity Partnership, provide platforms for that work. There is also a broader rationale. The bilateral relationship, which has long been described as the most consequential partnership for the United States, has been visibly strained in the past year over trade and other policy divergences, and critical minerals and technology could offer durable anchors in which interests are complementary rather than competitive. India's diplomatic reach across the Global South further gives it the ability to shape markets and standards well beyond its own resource base. Deeper U.S.-India cooperation on critical minerals therefore offers Washington the prospect of expanding coordination with a major Indo-Pacific power whose influence across emerging economies is poised to grow and has the potential to offer some balance to China’s economic and technological influence in the region.
Pakistan
Pakistan is the upstream bet, and its value depends on whether a large but still lightly appraised resource base can be turned into a small number of projects that reach production. The government has pointed to up to $8 trillion in untapped mineral resources. Pakistan commercially utilizes 52 of its 92 known minerals, yet mining accounts for only 3.2% of GDP. The nearest-term opportunities lie in copper, gold, and antimony. Rare earth potential is at an earlier stage and would need systematic geological assessments to establish the scale and viability of resources.
Reko Diq in Balochistan is the clearest test of Pakistan’s potential. It is one of the largest undeveloped copper-gold deposits in the world, relaunched in 2022 after a long legal dispute and is now owned 50% by Canada's Barrick, 25% by three Pakistani state-owned enterprises, and 25% by the Government of Balochistan. The project has drawn financing from the International Finance Corporation and the Asian Development Bank, and the United States announced around $1.3 billion in support in February 2026, led by the Export-Import Bank and as a part of Project Vault. Yet Barrick slowed planned activity earlier this year over security concerns and the regional risk profile tied to the Middle East conflict. articles.title: Africa Retains a mere 5% of the Massive $29.5 Trillion Critical Mineral Value it owns - GBC Ghana Online
articles.summary: Africa Retains a mere 5% of the Massive $29.5 Trillion Critical Mineral Value it owns  GBC Ghana Online
articles.full_text:
By: Franklin ASARE-DONKOH
Africa is home to a staggering $29.5 trillion in critical mineral wealth, yet the continent retains a mere 5% of its total economic value, according to African Union (AU) Commissioner for Economic Development, Tourism, Trade, Industry and Minerals, Francisca Tatchouop Belobe.
According to Tatchouop Belobe, Africa holds nearly 30% of the world’s critical mineral reserves and an estimated $29.5 trillion in mineral wealth, representing about 20% of the global total.
At the Mining in Motion Conference in Accra, Mrs Belobe critiqued the current global extraction model. In a sharp critique delivered by the African Union Commissioner for Economic Development, Tourism, Trade, Industry and Minerals it was noted that, the continent’s vast mineral resources had not translated into commensurate industrial development and economic prosperity.
She warned that, without radical reforms in domestic processing, local value addition, and policy enforcement, Africa will remain trapped in a cycle of resource exploitation that benefits foreign economies at the expense of Africa’s own people.
“It is painful that while other countries are building industries around Africa’s mineral resources, we continue to export them raw”
The Value Gap
The $29.5 trillion figure encompasses vast global reserves of cobalt, lithium, manganese, nickel, and graphite, minerals that are absolutely essential for the global transition to green energy, electric vehicles, and advanced electronics. In spite of hosting the lion’s share of these raw materials however, African nations see only a tiny fraction of the profits.
The vast majority of the financial windfall, industrial jobs, and technological advancements are also generated overseas, where the raw materials are refined and manufactured into high-value components.
“We are exporting our future in its rawest form. To receive only 5% of a multi-trillion-dollar wealth fund is not just an economic failure; it is an unsustainable model for a continent with the fastest-growing youth population in the world.” Belobe noted.
Breaking the “Resource Curse”
The report underscores a long-standing challenge known as the “resource curse,” where mineral-rich countries suffer from low economic development due to poor governance and a lack of industrial capacity.
To reverse the current trend, Mrs. Belobe and other economic experts are urging African governments to implement a series of structural shifts:
• Ban Raw Mineral Exports: Emulate countries like Zimbabwe and Namibia, which have instituted partial or full bans on exporting unprocessed lithium and crushed ore to force domestic processing.
• Establish Regional Value Chains: Develop cross-border processing hubs within Africa, allowing landlocked or smaller nations to send raw minerals to regional neighbours with advanced industrial infrastructure.
• Harmonise Mining Codes: Standardise tax, royalty, and environmental regulations across the African Union to prevent multinational corporations from playing nations against one another for cheaper extraction terms.
• Invest in Renewable Energy: Power local refineries with clean, domestic energy sources to ensure that Africa’s green mineral supply chain is sustainable from extraction to final product.
The challenge is, if the African Union can effectively engineer Sovereign African Nations to implement these measures, when they either lack the capacity to do so, or are beholden to exploitative powers who have historically succeeded in thwarting such measures, when in comes to Africa speaking with one voice.
A Call for Joint Action
As global demand for green technology intensifies, the window of opportunity for African nations to assert control over their supply chains is narrow. Mrs. Belobe concluded with an urgent call to action for the African Union and regional economic blocs to act as a unified negotiating power.
By refusing to sell unrefined minerals and demanding equity in the global tech ecosystem, the continent can turn its $29.5 trillion potential into tangible wealth, sustainable jobs, poverty reduction, infrastructure development and more.

articles.full_text:
As artificial intelligence (AI) advances from an experimental technology into a foundational layer of the global economy, attention has focused largely on its most visible physical constraints: electricity, data center capacity, and water for cooling. Yet the more consequential bottleneck may lie further upstream, in the minerals required to manufacture the semiconductors, power systems, transmission equipment, cooling infrastructure, and energy-storage technologies on which the AI economy depends.
These minerals are becoming increasingly vulnerable to supply-chain disruption for two interconnected reasons. First, AI is adding demand to materials already under pressure from other fast-growing industries, including electric vehicles, renewable energy, and semiconductor manufacturing. Second, the mining, refining and processing of these materials remain concentrated in a relatively small number of countries, leaving manufacturers and technology companies exposed to potential disruptions. China, for example, is the leading refiner for 19 of the 20 strategic minerals tracked by the International Energy Agency (IEA), with an average market share of around 70%.[1]
The emerging challenge is therefore larger than securing enough GPUs. The next phase of the AI race will be decided not only in chip-design labs and hyperscale data centers, but also in mines, refineries, power plants, and transmission corridors. Scaling AI increasingly depends on whether economies can build the physical infrastructure around compute and secure the copper, aluminum, gallium, germanium, rare earths and other materials needed to deliver it at speed.
This article explores: (i) how AI infrastructure is creating new sources of demand across critical mineral supply chains, (ii) where emerging bottlenecks and geographic concentrations could expose AI expansion to supply risks, (iii) how governments are responding through critical mineral strategies, export controls, domestic production, and supply-chain diversification, and (iv) how technology, mining, and infrastructure companies are adapting their investments. Together, these developments could make access to critical materials an increasingly important dimension of global AI competition.
Mapping AI’s material dependencies
As AI infrastructure expands, demand is rising not only for the specialized materials used in advanced electronics, but also for the industrial metals required to connect, power and cool these systems. The minerals underpinning that architecture can therefore be grouped into two broad categories: those needed directly for computing and communications, and those needed indirectly to build and operate the infrastructure that supports them. Directly needed minerals, including gallium and germanium, are used in semiconductors, high-performance electronics and fiber-optic communications. Gallium is used in compound semiconductors and high-performance power electronics, technologies that can operate at higher frequencies, temperatures, and voltages than conventional silicon-based components. Rare earth elements support the permanent magnets found in motors, cooling equipment, and other electrical systems used throughout data center infrastructure.
Indirectly needed minerals, most notably copper and aluminum, form the backbone of the power, cooling, transmission, and data center infrastructure that enables AI to operate at scale. Copper is the clearest example of how AI’s material footprint extends far beyond the server rack. Inside a data center, copper is used in cabling, busbars, power-distribution systems, cooling equipment, and electrical connections. Aluminum plays a similar role. Its lower weight and strong conductivity make it essential to transmission networks and electrical equipment, while its use in data center structures, heat-management systems and cooling infrastructure gives it a direct connection to the physical expansion of computing capacity.
Outside the facility, the requirements become even more substantial. Large-scale computing projects can require new substations, transformers, transmission lines, distribution upgrades, and dedicated generation capacity. In other words, AI does not merely consume electricity. It consumes the infrastructure required to deliver reliable electricity at scale. That distinction is becoming increasingly important as data centers grow larger and more concentrated. A single hyperscale campus can represent a major new industrial load, forcing utilities and developers to accelerate grid connections and expand equipment capacity. Every additional layer from the transmission network to the facility’s internal power systems adds to the demand for copper. While directly needed materials may be consumed in relatively small quantities compared with copper or aluminum, their strategic importance comes from the difficulty to substitute. These are often produced as by-products and processed through highly concentrated supply chains. A small physical requirement can therefore create a large commercial vulnerability if access is disrupted.
There is also another layer of indirect materials becoming increasingly relevant to AI data centers, and these are lithium, graphite and nickel. They enter the AI supply chain through a different route, namely energy storage. Data centers require uninterrupted power. As their electricity demand rises, operators and utilities are deploying larger battery systems to provide backup power, manage short-duration fluctuations, and support the integration of renewable energy. Batteries can also help reduce pressure on constrained grids by shifting electricity use or providing fast-response capacity during periods of peak demand. That makes AI infrastructure an indirect but increasingly important source of demand for battery materials. The connection is particularly significant in markets where data center developers are pursuing renewable power commitments or where grid reliability is insufficient to support rapid expansion without additional storage.
However, AI is unlikely to become the largest source of global demand for every material it touches. Electric vehicles, renewable energy systems, electricity networks, and battery storage remain larger consumers of several critical minerals. But AI is arriving at a moment when those sectors are already competing for the same supplies. Global lithium demand increased by almost 30% in 2024, while demand for nickel, cobalt, graphite, and rare earth elements rose by between 6% and 8%, according to the IEA.[2] Much of that growth was driven by electric vehicles, battery storage, renewable energy and grid investment. Therefore, the significance of AI lies less in its share of total mineral demand than in the timing, location, and concentration of the demand it adds and is considered a powerful new competitor.
The geography problem: location of minerals is only half the story
The countries leading the AI race are not necessarily the countries controlling the materials that make it possible. The United States dominates much of the AI software stack. American companies design the leading chips, build the largest cloud platforms, and are investing billions of dollars in new data centers. Europe is trying to secure a role in advanced computing and industrial AI. China is pursuing technological self-sufficiency at national scale.
But the physical supply chain behind that competition follows a very different map. Copper comes primarily from Chile, Peru, and the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC). Australia, Chile, China, and Argentina are central to the lithium supply. Guinea is a critical source of bauxite, the ore used to produce aluminum. DRC supplies most of the world’s mined cobalt.[3] Those countries may not control the AI platforms being built in Silicon Valley, Seattle, Beijing, or Paris. They control the raw materials without which the servers, power systems, batteries, transmission networks, and cooling equipment cannot be manufactured.
Even that description, however, is incomplete. Mining is only the first stage of the supply chain and often not the stage where the greatest strategic power resides. The decisive bottleneck is frequently found later, in refining, chemical conversion, separation, component manufacturing, and the production of materials that meet industrial specifications. A country may have the ore, but another country may control the technology, facilities, and commercial relationships needed to turn that ore into a usable input.
China has spent decades building precisely this kind of downstream capacity. Its influence is therefore much greater than its share of mining alone would suggest. In magnet rare earths, China accounted for roughly 60% of global mining in 2024, but about 91% of separation and refining and 94% of sintered permanent-magnet production, according to the IEA.[4]
That progression from mine to refinery to finished component is the real story. The material that leaves a mine is rarely the material purchased by a semiconductor manufacturer, battery producer, or data center equipment supplier. Between the two are processing plants, specialized chemical facilities, logistics networks, technical expertise, and years of accumulated industrial know-how. Recreating that system is expensive, slow, and often environmentally contentious. Gallium demonstrates why this matters for AI. It is not typically extracted from dedicated mines. Instead, it is recovered as a by-product of processing bauxite and zinc ores. Germanium is similarly tied to the processing of other mineral streams. If prices rise, producers cannot simply decide to open a new gallium or germanium mine. Supply depends on the economics and capacity of much larger industries and on whether the relevant refining infrastructure exists outside China.

As Australia strengthens its global critical minerals position, QME is set to bring the industry together to explore the technologies, partnerships and ideas shaping the next phase of resource development.
The sunshine state is no stranger to the mining industry, and the upcoming Queensland Mining and Engineering Expo (QME) is poised to be a crucial opportunity for sharing knowledge and information, with Australia leading the global landscape as a key critical minerals supplier. To be held at the Mackay Showgrounds from July 21–23, it remains the largest regional mining exhibition in Queensland.
This year’s event will again feature the Mining Pavilion, a central hub bringing together key companies and major contractors to showcase their latest projects. Prime Creative Media show director – mining events Rebecca Todesco said the pavilion remains one of the most highly anticipated features of QME.
“The Mining Pavilion has always been where the industry comes together,” she said.
“It gives visitors direct access to the people behind major operations, while giving mining companies a powerful platform to engage, share insights and build lasting connections.”
By placing operators alongside equipment manufacturers, engineering firms and technology developers, the pavilion offers a rare opportunity to see how new ideas move from concept to implementation. That kind of collaborative environment is particularly significant as the sector responds to rising global demand for critical minerals.
As demand accelerates across electrification, clean energy and defence technologies, QME 2026 arrives at a pivotal moment for Australia’s resources sector. From lithium and nickel to rare earths and graphite, these minerals are among the most strategically important segments of the mining industry.
Australia already holds some of the world’s largest reserves of many of these commodities, and growing exploration activity and processing innovation are positioning the country as a cornerstone supplier to international markets.
For Queensland, the opportunity continues to expand.
While the state remains synonymous with coal exports, new investments in battery metals and advanced processing are broadening the resources landscape, pushing companies and suppliers to rethink everything from extraction methods to refining technologies.
Now in its third decade, QME helps to brings those developments into focus by gathering the entire mining ecosystem under one roof.
Across the event’s exhibition floor, attendees can move between heavy equipment displays, digital mining platforms, mineral processing technologies and specialised services, offering a comprehensive view of how modern mine sites operate.
For companies pursuing critical minerals projects, this environment is particularly valuable.
Unlike traditional bulk commodities, critical minerals often require specialised processing pathways, including advanced flotation systems, hydrometallurgical refining techniques, and monitoring systems designed to maximise recovery rates. These technologies are essential for transforming raw ore into the battery-grade materials demanded by global supply chains.
At QME, those innovations are not confined to presentations or white papers. Instead, they are demonstrated live on the exhibition floor.
Beyond the machinery and displays, QME’s seminar sessions and leadership programs have historically drawn strong participation from industry experts and policymakers. Topics often range from the future of coal, metals and minerals; the push toward more sustainable mining; and the latest thinking in safety, mental health, and workforce wellbeing.
Hosting the exhibition in Mackay also places the event within one of Australia’s most established mining regions. The city has long served as a hub for mining services, engineering expertise and supply chain logistics supporting Queensland’s resources sector.
As the industry transitions into new commodities and technologies, Mackay continues to serve as a meeting point for operators, suppliers and innovators.
For three days in July, that convergence will place the region at the centre of the national mining conversation.
As Australia strengthens its position in the global critical minerals supply chain, gatherings like QME become more than exhibitions. They become a place where the industry can examine its future and where the conversations shaping that future begin.
Tickets are out now. Get your tickets at queenslandminingexpo.com.au/attendee-enquiries.

articles.title: The Race for Malaysia’s Rare Earths: An Indo-Pacific Strategy - CSIS | Center for Strategic and International Studies
articles.summary: The Race for Malaysia’s Rare Earths: An Indo-Pacific Strategy  CSIS | Center for Strategic and International Studies

source_detail.name: CSIS | Center for Strategic and International Studies

articles.full_text:
Introduction
As the United States and its closest allies race to diversify rare earth supply chains and establish nodes of production outside the sphere of dominance of China, Malaysia has emerged as a key player. At the center of Malaysia’s strategic importance is its refining capacity: In 2025, it became the first country outside of China to produce dysprosium oxide, a key heavy rare earth for the defense industry. Now, its processing capacity is set to expand precipitously with investment in a new facility, which will increase capacity from 1,500 metric tons of heavy rare earth feedstock to 5,000 metric tons per year.
This effort is spearheaded by Lynas Rare Earths, an Australian company that first received its license to operate in Gebeng, Malaysia, in 2012. Malaysia’s rise as a rare earth processing hub, while a significant triumph for Lynas, cannot be attributed to just one company or even one country. Rather, Malaysia’s development as a commercial-scale rare earth processor has been enabled by decades of international investment and commitment: Malaysia’s reform to its regulatory ecosystem, China’s infrastructure investment, Japan’s patient capital, Australia’s technological expertise, and the United States’ most recent offtake agreement and price support. Malaysia sits at the intersection of plurilateral efforts to diversify rare earth supply chains and serves as an example of how targeted support can transform countries with little experience in the rare earth industry into significant producers shifting the global landscape.
The successful commercial production of refined heavy rare earth metals outside of China is merely the beginning of global efforts to diversify mineral supply chains. The Malaysian government is spearheading efforts to turn the country into not just a landing pad for midstream investment by foreign firms but also an integrated contributor to global rare earth supply chains. Malaysia seeks to achieve this by both continuing to emphasize its industrial capacity as a processing hub and emphasizing technology transfer and research and development (R&D) up and down the supply chain. Malaysia holds the potential to be a major source of heavy rare earth feedstock from large ionic clay deposits. Its rare earth deposits are estimated at 16.1 million metric tons, the third-largest reserves in the world after China (44 million) and Brazil (21 million). Importantly, ionic clay deposits are nonradioactive, circumventing the social challenges that often arise from traditional hard-rock deposits that are colocated with potentially hazardous radioactive materials. This significant source of feedstock will become only more strategic as Malaysia increases its refining capacity over the next several years. The rare earth industry is expected to contribute as much as 9.5 billion MYR ($2 billion) to the country’s GDP in 2025 and create nearly 7,000 job opportunities.
China already has a head start. In 2022, MCRE Resources, a joint venture between Chinese and Malaysian stakeholders, began developing the Gerik ionic clay deposit in the state of Perak. Using Chinese in situ leaching technology, MCRE exported nearly $11 million worth of rare earth ore to China from January to September 2025 for refining. Without a competitive Western alternative, Malaysia will continue to rely on Chinese technology, equipment, know-how, refining capabilities, and offtake to unlock its rare earth resources.
China has only strengthened its position within Malaysia in recent years. In April 2025, when Malaysia was hit with a 24 percent reciprocal tariff from U.S. President Donald Trump, Chinese President Xi Jinping arrived in Kuala Lumpur on his first state visit to Malaysia in 13 years to meet with Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim. During the visit, Xi proclaimed a new “golden era” of China-Malaysia relations and signed a flurry of 31 agreements on railway transportation, semiconductors, aircraft sales, and agriculture. China has made large-scale, concrete investments in Malaysia’s economic future and mineral resources. In comparison, the United States has made softer commitments to Malaysia, offering introductory dialogues for engagement but no hard capital commitments. Malaysia is one of the only near-term suppliers outside China for materials the United States requires for global power projection. If the United States wishes to access these materials and counter China’s influence in the region, it needs a new strategy that pairs meaningful investment with coordinated diplomatic engagement.
This white paper reviews how Malaysia came to be a strategically valuable node in the rare earth supply chain and outlines the role and continuing influence of several international partners in fostering an enabling ecosystem for commercial-scale processing. The paper recommends a path forward to transforming Malaysia into a key U.S. partner in securing rare earth supply chains by leveraging existing ties between Malaysia and trilateral partners (Australia, Japan, and the United States). With critical mineral frameworks already underway between the United States, Australia, Japan, and Malaysia, now is the time to deepen industrial ties in the rare earth industry—before China secures the resources entirely for itself.
The Rise of Malaysia’s Rare Earth Industry
Malaysia has managed to successfully develop its rare earth processing sector over the course of decades. It has done so through both strategic domestic industrial policy planning and foreign policy engagement with a variety of neighbors in the Indo-Pacific region. As a result, Malaysia boasts an attractive regulatory regime, well-suited infrastructure, and conducive diplomatic relationships to attract investment from a breadth of international partners.
Malaysia’s mineral industry dates to the nineteenth century during Malaysia’s British colonial era. Discoveries of large tin deposits in the states of Perak and Selangor ushered in large amounts of capital investment from China and Europe, along with Chinese migrant workers and European technology. By 1904, Malaysia supplied 50 percent of the world’s tin. While Malaysia remained a significant supplier of tin to Europe throughout World Wars I and II, its share of global production declined steadily throughout the second half of the twentieth century as other major producers, including Indonesia, Bolivia, and Peru, entered the market. By the 1990s, tin exports accounted for less than 1 percent of Malaysia’s economy. Nevertheless, Malaysia’s history of tin mining played a significant role in launching its rare earth processing industry, as leftover tin by-products offered feedstock for early rare earth enterprises.
The country’s first rare earth operation began in 1982, with a monazite processing plant in Bukit Merah operated by Asian Rare Earths, a Mitsubishi subsidiary. The plant repurposed slag from old tin smelting operations to extract rare earths within the feedstock. However, the endeavor ended in catastrophe. Residents and workers near the plant raised the alarm that radioactive materials and waste could be responsible for a notable spike in birth defects and cancer rates in the small community. The project was permanently closed in 1992, followed by years of site cleanup.
This tragic history continues to shape public attitudes in Malaysia toward the rare earth industry, even decades later. Lynas received approval from the Malaysian government to build its facility within an industrial park in 2007, but years of vocal opposition, protests, and legal filings by the Stop Lynas movement delayed operations until 2012. As a result, the Malaysian government has had to tread carefully as it crafts its critical minerals strategy, balancing incentives for foreign investments with environmental regulations and oversight.
Critical Minerals Regulation in Malaysia
Malaysia first undertook efforts to formalize its minerals policy landscape in 1994 with the original National Mineral Policy (NMP1) to lay the groundwork for a robust and competitive regulatory environment for the minerals sector. The industry is governed by the Mineral Development Act of 1994, which delineates the powers of the federal government to regulate mineral exploration and mining while the state governments maintain the power to issue mineral exploration and mining licenses. Each state sets its own regulations for mining activities and may impose royalties. The act also mandates adherence to health and safety regulations to protect workers and communities near mining sites.
The National Mineral Policy was updated in 2009 (NMP2), identifying areas of focus, or “strategic thrusts,” including expanding the mineral resource sector, fostering a conducive business climate for investment, and enhancing R&D efforts. The new framework introduced standardized model mineral agreements between states and investors to establish baseline legal and commercial terms and environmental standards across jurisdictions. It also sought to attract foreign investment through security of tenure policies, transparent implementation of state mineral legislation, and fiscal incentives. Lynas received a 12-year tax holiday as a “pioneer investor” in the burgeoning rare earth industry, making Malaysia a highly cost-competitive jurisdiction for investment compared to Australia or other regional destinations.
Malaysian minerals policy consistently prioritizes the development of midstream processing and greater value-added industries over extractive industries. Malaysia has a large services sector, accounting for 59.5 percent of GDP, and a relatively small manufacturing sector, making up just 23 percent of GDP in 2025. Malaysia views the transition to technology-driven industrialization as the key to unlocking further economic growth and welcomes foreign direct investments to transfer new skills and technologies as a pivotal shortcut to value-added production. Key Highlights
- Sterling Metals Corp. recorded a 5.56% decline on October 20, 2026, reflecting secondary market distribution, tactical position trimming following multi-month trading advances, and heightened multiple sensitivity across Canadian-listed junior copper and base metal exploration equities.
- Headquartered in Toronto, Ontario, and listed on the TSX Venture Exchange under the ticker symbol SAG (with quotations on the OTCQB under SAGGF and Frankfurt under 4S0), the company focuses on acquiring, exploring, and delineating district-scale copper, silver, and polymetallic assets in Tier 1 Canadian mining camps.
- The company’s exploration asset foundation is anchored by its flagship Soo Copper Project in Ontario—where multi-rig drilling continues to test the MEPS copper discovery zone—alongside the district-scale Adeline sediment-hosted copper-silver project in Labrador and newly consolidated regional acreage acquired via the QcX Gold transaction.
- Operating as an early-stage exploration enterprise generating no commercial mining revenue or operational cash flows, the corporation's enterprise valuation remains heavily tethered to diamond drill assay disclosures, geological target delineation, and continuous public equity capital access.
- The single-session pullback highlights investor sensitivity regarding step-out drill assay delivery intervals, analytical laboratory turnaround lead times, and exploration treasury runway against an elevated baseline cost-of-capital environment.

Introduction
Sterling Metals Corp. (TSXV:SAG) is an early-stage mineral exploration and resource development enterprise listed on the TSX Venture Exchange. Headquartered in Toronto, Ontario, the corporation is dedicated to creating long-term shareholder value through the systematic discovery, geochemical mapping, geophysical imaging, and multi-phase diamond drilling of district-scale copper, silver, and polymetallic assets across premier Canadian jurisdictions. The organization's exploration portfolio is led by the flagship Soo Copper Project, where active multi-rig drilling is delineating the MEPS porphyry discovery across expanding strike lengths. In addition, the company holds the district-scale Adeline project in Labrador, prospective for sediment-hosted stratabound copper and silver mineralization across extensive volcanic and sedimentary corridors, complemented by regional claim consolidations in Ontario. Rather than operating commercial milling infrastructure or extracting active commercial ores, the enterprise creates shareholder value through advanced geological modeling, induced polarization geophysics, and diamond core drilling. Consequently, the organization's corporate velocity, balance sheet runway, and public equity valuation depend directly on core drill assay disclosures, geological model continuity, capital market access, and broader trading sentiment across the global copper and critical minerals complexes.
On October 20, 2026, Sterling Metals Corp. common shares concluded trading lower, registering a 5.56% decline on the TSX Venture Exchange. A single-session contraction of this magnitude extends recent secondary market consolidation across intermediate base metal exploration equities. Rather than an isolated technical reset, the retreat reflects ongoing institutional scrutiny regarding exploration pacing, the lead times required to convert newly drilled intervals into compliant mineral resource estimates, and the defensibility of exploration-stage multiples in an elevated baseline cost-of-capital environment.
The broader junior mining and copper exploration backdrop presents distinct cyclical hurdles alongside secular energy transition tailwinds. While long-term macroeconomic demand for copper remains supported by power grid modernization, renewable infrastructure buildouts, and structural primary supply deficits, early-stage exploration equities frequently encounter extended periods of institutional disengagement. Upstream exploration developers face rising specialized diamond drilling day rates, persistent cost inflation across technical field labor, and selective equity financing conditions. Compounding these dynamics, elevated baseline borrowing yields and competitive sovereign bond returns have narrowed institutional risk tolerance, prompting market participants to demand demonstrable geological validation and prudent treasury management before assigning sustained valuation premiums to emerging exploration platforms.
Key Reasons Behind Decline
The primary catalyst driving the October 20, 2026 decline centers on continuous secondary market distribution, tactical position trimming following previous trading advances, and cautious institutional portfolio rebalancing across Canadian-listed junior copper exploration equities:
- Weak investor sentiment: Investor sentiment remains an acute headwind across junior mineral exploration platforms. When broader financial market volatility expands, institutional portfolio managers routinely trim exposure to pre-revenue developers that lack self-funding operating cash flows, generating sustained downward pressure on share prices.
- Sector weakness across junior base and precious metals peers: Base metal and junior copper exploration peer groups have experienced widespread valuation compression. Market participants continue to differentiate sharply between established, cash-flowing senior mining producers and early-stage exploration assets whose commercial potential lies in distant operating cycles.
- Operational challenges and exploration execution dynamics: Advancing multi-rig diamond drilling campaigns across extensive regional claim packages in Ontario requires ongoing contractor coordination, surface access logistics, camp management, and specialized core logging. Exploration across complex porphyry systems is inherently subject to structural variability, where complex fault offsets, variable fracture densities, or localized grade pinching can introduce analytical delays.
- Poor execution risks and timeline friction: Exploration cycles demand continuous technical updates to sustain market confidence. Extended turnaround times at commercial analytical laboratories or wide intervals between drill assay releases can test market patience and prompt tactical profit-taking following periods of strong share appreciation.
- The weaker demand outlook for pre-commercial resource assets: Cautious capital market conditions for early-stage mining assets have prompted periodic reassessments of exploration velocity, with institutional allocators remaining guarded regarding the multi-year capital required to advance raw discoveries into compliant mineral resources.
- Macroeconomic pressure and interest rate dynamics: Elevated benchmark borrowing costs and sovereign bond yields create competitive hurdles against non-yielding, speculative resource equities, keeping institutional capital cautious and raising required equity return thresholds.
- Commodity volatility across copper benchmarks: Swings in spot and forward copper prices directly govern modeled cut-off grades and net asset values, amplifying equity volatility during commodity price consolidations. For junior developers, revisions in assumed commodity pricing lead to outsized adjustments in market-implied asset valuations.
- Declining earnings visibility during exploration cycles: Because the enterprise generates no recurring commercial mining revenues, traditional price-to-earnings and cash-flow multiples provide no valuation floor, leaving the equity susceptible to sharp sentiment resets between exploration releases.
- Margin concerns and underlying field cost inflation: Rising specialized diamond drilling day rates, skilled technical labor wages, core assay charges, and remote transport logistics elevate corporate cash burn, dampening capital deployment efficiency.
- Funding pressure and capital allocation discipline: Advancing extensive multi-rig diamond drilling programs alongside regional ground consolidation requires continuous treasury replenishment; in restrictive capital markets, securing project funding creates ongoing dilution sensitivities.
- Speculative selling and micro-cap liquidity constraints: In specialized Canadian venture issues characterized by moderate daily trading volume, relatively small institutional block reallocations or automated stop-loss executions can produce an outsized negative impact on share-price discovery.
- Institutional outflows: Institutional asset managers have continued rotating capital toward large-cap senior copper producers to reduce portfolio tracking error and single-asset exploration risk during periods of broader financial market volatility.
- Geopolitical tensions: Persistent international friction, including Middle East conflicts involving the United States and Iran, creates systemic volatility across global energy benchmarks, shipping corridors, and financial markets. While heightened geopolitical instability reinforces the strategic necessity of secure Western critical mineral supplies, it simultaneously fuels inflationary cost pressures on operating fuel, mechanical supplies, and transport logistics, while prompting institutional allocators to adopt defensive postures and trim speculative resource holdings.

articles.full_text:
Between now and 2050, the lithium industry will need the equivalent of 134 new lithium mines to keep pace with rising demand for the critical mineral. Of these, 44 are needed to meet demand growth between 2040 and 2050 alone.
Benchmark Mineral Intelligence forecasts that global lithium demand will reach ~7 million tonnes of lithium carbonate equivalent (LCE) in 2050, with 76% of this driven by electric vehicles.
This is an increase of 4.8 million tonnes from a demand of 2.11 million tonnes LCE in 2026. At an average mine size of 36,000 tonnes LCE, this growth is equivalent to the output of 134 new mines – effectively a new mine every two months for the next 24 years.
“Meeting 2050 demand requires the equivalent of 134 new lithium mines, more than US$100 billion of investment before any contribution from recycling, rising to more than 180 mines in our upside scenario,” said Cameron Perks, Product Director – Lithium at Benchmark. “The biggest challenge is sustaining that investment through price cycles, while competing for capital with AI, defence and the wider energy transition.”
What is driving lithium demand?
Between 2026 and 2050, lithium demand is forecast to more than triple, with the vast majority of this growth driven by the battery market.
Batteries account for 92% of lithium demand in 2026, up from around 70% in 2020. Electric vehicles currently account for 55% of lithium demand, and this is forecast to grow to 76% by 2050 as the rapid recent growth in stationary storage moderates.
“Lithium demand from stationary storage has grown more than 60% a year for the past two years, but we expect that pace to slow significantly, to around 5% a year to the end of the decade,” Perks said.
Where is lithium mined?
Australia is forecast to be the largest producer of mined lithium in 2026, accounting for 29% of mined supply. However, Australia’s share of forecast mine supply is set to fall to 20% by 2050, even with large-scale brownfield expansions such as PLS’s P2000 factored in for a start around 2030.
“Many of Australia’s mines will be depleting by 2050. Price volatility has made financiers hesitant, and the regulatory burden is growing,” Perks said. “It’s not too late, but if Australia doesn’t back growth, other regions will take that share.”
In contrast, China’s share is set to remain relatively stable at around 25%, supported by continued investment in domestic resources and an emphasis on battery supply chain dominance.
North American supply is set to increase from 1.7% of mined supply in 2026 to 13% by 2050, as the region works to meet its own domestic requirements and reduce reliance on China. North America currently accounts for 6% of lithium demand from cell production, which is forecast to increase to 12% by 2050.
Europe is similarly targeting domestic and allied supply chain development. The region currently accounts for less than 1% of mined supply, despite accounting for 7% of lithium demand from cell production. By 2050, 5.5% of mined lithium is forecast to come from Europe, compared with 8% of demand.
“Europe and North America face their own unique challenges,” Perks added. “Many of the largest and most promising projects require novel technology or face environmental and community concerns. These aren’t insurmountable, but they create significant delays, and they mean mines built in these regions simply cost more.”
What could impact this number?
This analysis assumes Benchmark’s base case. The number of mines could be significantly higher if the upside scenario of almost nine million tonnes LCE of demand is realised, driven largely by EV and energy storage policies worldwide.
“In our upside case, the equivalent number of mines rises to around 180, which would require well over US$150 billion,” Perks said. “And even the base-case investment could prove conservative, depending on where the mines are built.”
Recycling is the biggest factor that could reduce the number of new mines needed. Benchmark forecasts recycling will account for almost half of lithium supply by 2050. Benchmark’s capex analysis, which assumes recycling meets a significant share of future demand, puts the investment needed to meet 2040 lithium demand at around US$64 billion.
“Recycling will grow, but our base case asks a lot of it,” Perks said. “It’s limited by how quickly batteries reach end of life, and it still needs to compete with mines on cost. Every tonne that recycling doesn’t deliver has to come from a mine.”

American Battery Technology NASDAQ: ABAT is advancing a U.S.-based battery-materials strategy built around lithium-ion battery recycling and the development of its Tonopah Flats Lithium Project in Nevada, Chief Financial Officer Alex Flores said during a company presentation.
Flores said the company is seeking to build a domestic, lower-cost and environmentally responsible supply chain for battery metals, including lithium, nickel, cobalt and manganese. He cited supply-security concerns, logistics costs and environmental risks associated with overseas sourcing as major challenges for the U.S. battery industry.
“Our approach is to first close the loop and then fill the loop,” Flores said, referring to the company’s recycling operations and its planned lithium mining and refining operations.
Recycling Operations and Expansion Plans
American Battery Technology operates a 138,000-square-foot lithium-ion battery recycling facility outside Reno, Nevada, with annual intake capacity of 20,000 metric tons. Operations at the site began in October 2023, according to Flores.
The company’s recycling process first dismantles battery packs into modules, cells and sub-cell components. It separates materials including copper, aluminum and steel, while producing a lithium-bearing intermediate known as black mass. In a subsequent refining phase, the company said the material can be processed into battery-grade nickel sulfate, manganese sulfate, cobalt sulfate and lithium hydroxide.
Flores said the company currently sees stronger economics in selling black mass than in further refining it into lithium products. He said a federal directive issued on Aug. 27 banned black-mass exports, but American Battery Technology received a license allowing it to export up to $100 million of the material.
The company is not selling black mass to China, Flores said, adding that its customers are primarily in South Korea and other OECD countries.
American Battery Technology also plans to build a second recycling facility in the southeastern U.S. The proposed site would have annual intake capacity of 100,000 metric tons, representing a five-fold increase from the Reno facility’s capacity. Flores said the project has received a Department of Energy grant equivalent to $150 million and is expected to require total capital expenditures of $375 million. The funding is a grant rather than a loan and carries performance milestones, he said.
Tonopah Lithium Project
On the mining side, the company is developing its Tonopah Flats Lithium Project near Tonopah, Nevada. Flores said the project encompasses 631 unpatented lode mining claims covering more than 13,000 acres and is based on a claystone lithium resource rather than conventional ore.
According to Flores, the project contains 21.3 million tons of accessible lithium hydroxide monohydrate and has a projected 45-year mine life. The company expects the operation to employ more than 200 full-time workers and reach a peak mining rate near 30,000 tons per day.
Flores cited the company’s pre-feasibility study, published about a year ago, which estimated an after-tax internal rate of return of 21.8%, net present value of $2.6 billion and production costs of slightly more than $4,300 per metric ton of lithium hydroxide monohydrate. Planned infrastructure includes a surface mine, commercial refinery and a behind-the-meter solar field with battery energy storage.
The project has received a $900 million letter of interest from the Export-Import Bank, Flores said. It has also been designated a priority project under the FAST-41 permitting framework. The company has initiated a definitive feasibility study, completed required National Environmental Policy Act baseline studies and submitted results to the Bureau of Land Management.
Flores said the Bureau of Land Management approved the company’s mining and refining plan of operations, which American Battery Technology had been developing since November 2022. The company was awaiting a notice of intent from the agency before moving into the environmental impact statement process. Under its expectations for the FAST-41 process, Flores said the company could break ground by the middle of the following year.
Financial Results and Domestic Supply Focus
Flores said American Battery Technology reported record fiscal 2026 revenue of $21.7 million, up 407% year over year. Cost of goods sold increased 67%, which he attributed to operational efficiencies at the Nevada recycling facility. The company reported cash-basis gross profit of $1.7 million, a non-GAAP figure excluding non-cash items such as depreciation and stock compensation.
The company ended the fiscal year with $49.5 million in cash and no debt, Flores said.
He also said American Battery Technology has operated a multi-ton-per-year integrated pilot facility that produced battery-grade lithium from Nevada claystone. The company is now pursuing strategic partners and long-term commercial offtake agreements as it seeks to expand its role in the North American battery-materials supply chain.
About American Battery Technology (NASDAQ:ABAT)
American Battery Technology Company develops technologies and operates projects intended to support a domestic battery-materials supply chain. The company focuses on lithium-ion battery recycling, lithium extraction from unconventional resources such as claystone, and the production of battery-grade materials for use in new batteries.
Its recycling business is designed to recover lithium, nickel, cobalt, manganese and other valuable materials from end-of-life batteries and manufacturing scrap.
